name: Shaving soap / cream
lead: Shaving soap and shaving cream are lubricating products applied to the face before razor shaving to soften hair through hydration and reduce friction.[1][2] Forms include hard soap bars or sticks and tubed lather creams that are worked into lather with a brush, brushless creams, aerosol foams and gels.[1]
Grokipedia states that the products are meant to reduce nicks and irritation.[2] No clinical trial of shaving soaps or creams for skin or appearance outcomes was found.
infobox: Shaving lubricant: soap, lather cream, brushless cream, aerosol foam, gel
Wood alkali and animal fat, Sumer, c. 3000 BC

paras: Lather creams usually contain 20 to 30 percent soap (potassium or triethanolamine), up to about 10 percent glycerine, plus emollients, emulsifiers and foaming agents, and a humectant keeps the lather moist.[1] Latherless creams are oil-in-water emulsions without soap, aerosol foams are diluted lather creams with hydrocarbon propellants, and gels were developed in the 1970s.[1] In 1993 Procter and Gamble patented a post-foaming gel that foams on the skin.[1] Preparations for electric shavers contain 50 to 80 percent alcohol to dry the skin and stiffen hair.[1]

A rudimentary precursor combining wood alkali and animal fat was used in Sumer around 3000 BC.[1] Hard shaving soaps were common in the early 20th century, followed by tubes of oil and soft-soap compounds.[1] Frank Shields developed the first shaving cream, sold as Barbasol, in 1919, and Rise, the first pressurised cream, appeared in 1949; pressurised products reached about two-thirds of the American market in the 1950s.[1] Chlorofluorocarbon propellants were banned in the late 1990s over ozone concerns and replaced with hydrocarbon mixtures.[1]
No studies found of shaving soaps or creams as appearance or skin interventions. Related laboratory physics work uses shaving foam as a model colloid and is not about skin effects.

Wikipedia notes that alcohol-heavy products dry the skin.[1] Aerosol products contain flammable hydrocarbon propellants, offset in cream formulations by high water content.[1] No studies of allergy or irritation from shaving products specifically were found.
No looksmaxxing forum material specific to shaving soap or cream was found.

timeline.event: Sumerians use a mixture of wood alkali and animal fat for shaving.[1]
Frank Shields develops Barbasol, the first brushless shaving cream.[1]
Rise, the first pressurised shaving cream, is introduced.[1]
Procter and Gamble patents a post-foaming shaving gel.[1]

card.summary: Lubricating soaps, creams, foams and gels for razor shaving; the aim is less friction, but no trials test it.
card.aka: shaving foam, shaving gel, shave soap
card.note: Alcohol-based and aerosol products can dry skin or be flammable.

quick.overview:
Shaving soap and cream coat the beard and skin so a razor glides with less friction. They come as bars, tubed creams, aerosol foams and gels, and have existed in some form since ancient Sumer.

Reference works describe their purpose as softer hair and less irritation, but no clinical studies were found.
quick.mechanism: Soap or surfactant, glycerine and emollients hydrate and soften hair and form a lubricating lather or film between blade and skin.
quick.risks: Alcohol-rich products dry the skin; aerosol cans use flammable propellants. No studies of product-specific irritation were found.
